title: Where Does School Segregation Come From?
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman responds to news that the Justice Department ended more than 50 school desegregation cases by asking where school segregation actually originates. He separates three sources: within-district segregation shaped by assignment policies, between-district segregation produced by housing and district boundaries, and between-state differences driven by population and economic patterns. Drawing on a 2022 study by Heewon Jang of racial economic segregation from 1991 to 2020, he reports that 59% comes from variation between districts, 26% from within districts, and 16% from between states. Regional examples sharpen the point: 88% of segregation in the Newark area and 76% in the Northeast overall is between districts, versus 41% in the South, where large countywide systems dominate. His conclusion is that ending court oversight will likely worsen within-district integration, but the largest levers are cross-district tools such as open enrollment, regional magnet schools, boundary changes, and housing policy.
points: Aldeman distinguishes within-district, between-district, and between-state segregation, and argues that the headline about ended court cases speaks only to the smallest-reaching of these.
Jang's study attributes 59% of racial economic segregation to differences between districts, 26% to differences within districts, and 16% to differences between states.
The balance varies by region: between-district differences account for 76% of racial segregation in the Northeast but just 41% in the South, where countywide districts blend cities and suburbs.
In Newark, 88% of segregation occurs between districts, and charter schools contribute only 0.03%, which undercuts segregation as an argument against charter growth there.
The policy implication is that open enrollment, regional magnets, boundary redesign, and housing policy that opens high-opportunity neighborhoods matter more than preserving within-district orders.
quotes: Despite the age of these cases, an investigation by K-12 Dive found that nearly half of those that were dismissed involved areas that were more racially segregated than they had been three decades earlier.
Between-district segregation is a different problem. Imagine a predominantly white suburban district bordering a predominantly Black urban district.
Even if every school within each of the two districts perfectly reflected the district’s own demographics, the greater metropolitan area would remain highly segregated.
That’s because the biggest component of racial economic segregation, by far, is between districts. Think of these as housing and district boundary issues, and they contribute 59% of the total.
In fact, the Century Foundation found that between-district differences accounted for 76% of racial segregation in the Northeast, compared with just 41% in the South.

So if policymakers want to address the largest source of segregation, especially in the Northeast and the Midwest, they would need to pursue things like open enrollment, regional magnet schools, changes to district boundaries, or housing policies that allow more families to live in high-opportunity neighborhoods.
Preserving integration within districts matters too, but most of the policies that could have the biggest effect on integration are ones that cross district boundaries.
